title: Down Syndrome (Trisomy 21)
subject: Paediatrics
summary: Down syndrome is a chromosomal disorder caused by an extra copy of chromosome 21. It presents with characteristic facial features, hypotonia, growth delay and a high prevalence of congenital heart disease. Management focuses on early detection of complications and multidisciplinary support.

sections.p: Down syndrome is a genetic condition caused by a full, translocation or mosaic extra chromosome 21. Diagnosis is confirmed by karyotype or rapid DNA‑based tests (e.g., QF‑PCR).
b: Full trisomy 21 ≈ 95 % of cases
Robertsonian translocation ≈ 3‑4 %
Mosaicism ≈ 1‑2 %

t.b: Confirms the type of trisomy; a result showing 47,XX,+21 or 47,XY,+21 confirms full trisomy.
Detects extra chromosome 21 quickly; a positive result is diagnostic in >99 % of cases.

sections.p: Severity is not staged by a numeric system but by the presence of major organ involvement, especially cardiac, gastrointestinal and neuro‑developmental deficits.
b: Mild: no major organ malformations, normal growth velocity
Moderate: congenital heart disease, feeding difficulties, moderate developmental delay
Severe: complex heart disease, severe hypotonia, refractory seizures or severe intellectual disability

sections.p: The extra chromosome originates from nondisjunction during meiosis, most often in the maternal oocyte; advanced maternal age is the strongest risk factor.
b: Maternal age >35 years – risk rises exponentially
Robertsonian translocation (often inherited from a parent carrier)
Mosaicism – post‑zygotic error

sections.p: Newborns show hypotonia, a single palmar crease, up‑slanting palpebral fissures and a flat nasal bridge. Early growth failure and feeding problems are common. Congenital heart disease (AVSD, VSD, PDA) occurs in ~45 % of infants.
b: Facial dysmorphism: flat face, epicanthal folds, small ears
Hypotonia → poor suck, failure to thrive
Single transverse palmar crease
Congenital heart lesions (AVSD most typical)

sections.p: Targeted tests identify associated anomalies and monitor complications that are common in low‑resource settings.

t.b: Detects structural heart disease; guides need for surgery or medical therapy.
Looks for macrocytosis, anemia, or leukopenia; macrocytosis is typical but anemia is not obligatory.
Screen for autoimmune thyroid disease, which is more prevalent in Down syndrome.
Identifies conductive or sensorineural loss; early intervention improves language development.

t.a: If echocardiography unavailable – clinical cardiac exam + chest X‑ray
t.b: Detects cardiomegaly, pulmonary congestion; refer for surgical assessment if signs of heart failure.

sections.p: Complications that may rapidly become life‑threatening require urgent attention.
b: Severe cyanosis or heart failure from uncorrected AVSD
Obstructive sleep apnea with recurrent apnoeas
Acute leukemia (especially ALL) – new lymphadenopathy, bruising
Severe hypothyroidism – lethargy, constipation, cold intolerance

sections.p: Management is multidisciplinary: treat cardiac lesions, support nutrition, monitor for endocrine and haematologic complications, and provide early developmental interventions.
b: Surgical repair of AVSD/VSD/PDA when indicated – reduces mortality
Feeding support: nasogastric tube or gastrostomy if severe hypotonia
Thyroid replacement (levothyroxine) for hypothyroidism – avoids neurocognitive delay
Regular screening for acute lymphoblastic leukaemia – CBC every 6 months in high‑risk settings
Vaccination according to national schedule; extra vigilance for respiratory infections

sections.p: Lifelong surveillance focuses on cardiac status, growth, neurodevelopment and endocrine health. Preventive care includes immunisations, early hearing/vision correction and parental education.
b: Cardiology review every 6‑12 months until cardiac lesion is closed
Growth monitoring at each clinic visit; address feeding issues early
Developmental therapy (physio, speech, occupational) from infancy
Annual thyroid function test; earlier if symptoms appear

sections.p: Conditions that share facial features or developmental delay may be mistaken for Down syndrome.
b: Turner syndrome – short stature and webbed neck but female only, no extra chromosome 21
Williams syndrome – “elfin” facies, hypercalcaemia, supravalvular aortic stenosis
Fetal alcohol spectrum – similar facial dysmorphism but history of maternal alcohol use

sections.p: Certain laboratory or clinical findings may appear normal despite underlying disease.
b: Normal haemoglobin despite macrocytosis – anemia may develop later
Mild cardiac murmur without echocardiography – can miss a significant septal defect
TSH slightly elevated in early hypothyroidism – repeat testing needed

whenToSeekHelp: Newborn with cyanosis, poor perfusion or severe respiratory distress
Sudden onset of lethargy, pallor or bruising – possible leukaemia
Rapid weight loss or feeding intolerance despite support

faq.q: Why is maternal age such a strong risk factor?
faq.a: Older oocytes have spent decades arrested in meiosis I, increasing the chance of nondisjunction that creates an extra chromosome 21.

faq.q: Do all children with Down syndrome need heart surgery?
faq.a: Only those with significant structural lesions (e.g., AVSD, large VSD) require repair; mild defects may be managed medically.

faq.q: Is there a cure for Down syndrome?
faq.a: No; treatment aims to optimise health, development and quality of life through early intervention and complication management.

exam: What immediate investigations would you order for a newborn with suspected Down syndrome and a harsh systolic murmur? — Echocardiography to define cardiac anatomy; CBC and thyroid tests as baseline screening.

How does the presence of an AVSD change your management plan compared with an isolated VSD? — AVSD usually requires earlier surgical repair due to risk of pulmonary hypertension; VSD may be observed if small.

A 3‑year‑old with Down syndrome presents with lethargy and constipation; TSH is 8 µIU/mL (normal 0.4‑4). What is your next step? — Start levothyroxine after confirming free T4 is low; monitor growth and development.
Explain why macrocytosis is common in Down syndrome even without anaemia. — The extra chromosome affects folate metabolism and bone‑marrow maturation, leading to larger red cells.

In a low‑resource setting without echocardiography, how would you identify a child who needs urgent cardiac referral? — Look for signs of heart failure: tachypnoea, hepatomegaly, feeding difficulty, and a loud murmur; obtain chest X‑ray for cardiomegaly.

What are the key components of the multidisciplinary follow‑up plan for a child with Down syndrome? — Cardiology, nutrition, developmental therapy, endocrine screening, hearing/vision checks, and immunisation updates.
Why is early screening for acute lymphoblastic leukaemia important in Down syndrome? — They have a 10‑20‑fold higher risk; early detection improves survival.

Distinguish the facial features of Down syndrome from those of Williams syndrome. — Down: flat nasal bridge, epicanthal folds, single palmar crease; Williams: broad forehead, full cheeks, “elfin” appearance, often with a wide mouth.
